measurementNotes: Specific reference measurements for the named species. A tilde (~) marks an approximation, rounded sample mean, or supported model estimate. Length labels distinguish bodies, shells, discs, arms, and tubes. School-card measurements describe one animal. Values are not a uniform series of maxima; gallery notes explain each reference. Unknown is retained only where a defensible weight was not located.

humpback-whale.description: Humpback whales sing long, evolving songs that can travel for miles. They team up to “bubble-net” feed, herding fish into a gulp with giant pleated throats.

oceanic-manta-ray.description: Manta rays glide on giant wings, funneling plankton with their head fins. They also visit cleaning stations where small fish remove parasites.

ocean-sunfish.description: Among the heaviest bony fish, ocean sunfish feed on jellyfish and other prey. They visit cleaning stations where fish pick off parasites.

whale-shark.description: Whale sharks are gentle giants—the largest fish on Earth—filtering plankton and tiny fish with a wide, sieve-like mouth.

blue-whale.description: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to live on Earth, a massive yet graceful marine mammal that glides through the open ocean.

basking-shark.description: Despite their colossal size, these gentle giants consume tiny zooplankton by simply swimming with their cavernous mouths wide open.

megamouth-shark.description: This rare shark filters tiny prey, including krill, through its enormous mouth. Its pale upper lip reflects light; it does not produce its own glow.

manta-ray.description: Reef manta rays filter plankton with their head fins and visit cleaning stations. Unique patterns of belly spots help researchers identify individuals.

hammerhead.description: They use their wide heads to sweep the ocean floor like a metal detector. They use thousands of tiny electrical sensors to find buried creatures.

great-white.description: An apex hunter that shapes the whole food web. Built for ambush: countershaded body hides it in sunlit seas.

bull-shark.description: Bull sharks can live in both salt and freshwater, cruising far up rivers—even hundreds of miles inland.

tiger-shark.description: A large, powerful predator found in warm ocean waters around the world, it has a broad diet and a reputation as an opportunistic hunter.

killer-whale-oceanic.description: Orcas are the largest members of the dolphin family. Their close-knit groups use different hunting traditions to catch fish, seals, or other whales.

pilot-whale-oceanic.description: Pilot whales live in close-knit pods led by experienced females. Deep divers, they chase squid in the dark and keep tight social bonds.

bottlenose-dolphin.description: Bottlenose dolphins are intelligent, social marine mammals with sleek gray bodies and short snouts. They use echolocation to find prey.

giant-squid.description: With enormous eyes adapted to dim light, giant squid roam the ocean depths. Two long feeding tentacles reach out to snatch fish and other squid.

colossal-squid.description: The heaviest known squid lives in the cold Southern Ocean. Rotating hooks on its tentacle clubs help it hold slippery prey.

greenland-shark.description: A slow-moving deep-water apex predator famous for having the longest known lifespan of all vertebrate animals.

giant-phantom-jelly.description: Unlike most jellyfish, the giant phantom jelly lacks stinging tentacles. Instead, it uses its long arms to trap plankton and small fish.
giant-phantom-jelly.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

sperm-whale.description: The largest toothed predators on Earth, sperm whales hunt for giant squid in the ocean deep using incredibly loud echolocation clicks.

shortfin-mako-shark.description: A powerful, fast-swimming shark, the shortfin mako pursues fish and squid. It can retain heat in parts of its body to stay active in cool water.

black-marlin.description: Black marlin hunt fish and squid with a long, spear-like bill. Their rigid pectoral fins cannot fold flat against the sides of the body.

swordfish.description: Charging through the pitch-black twilight zone, the swordfish uses its razor-sharp bill to slash and stun fast-moving schools of squid and fish.

bluefin-tuna.description: Atlantic bluefin tuna retain heat in their muscles and other tissues. This helps them pursue prey across both cool and warm ocean waters.

great-barracuda.description: Barracudas hover like steel spears, then explode forward in a silver blur to snatch prey with dagger teeth. They are drawn to flashes of light.

green-moray-eel.description: Moray eels lurk in crevices. They snatch prey, then fire out a second set of jaws (pharyngeal jaws) to pull it down.

reef-shark.description: Blacktip reef sharks are shallow-reef sprinters with signature black-tipped fins. They dart through lagoons at dawn and dusk, snapping up small fish.

goliath-grouper.description: Groupers are ambush hunters that gulp prey with a sudden vacuum from their huge mouths. They lurk in shadows, waiting for prey.

green-sea-turtle.description: Adult green turtles graze mainly on seagrass and algae. After long ocean migrations, females return to their natal nesting regions to lay eggs.

spinner-dolphins.description: Spinner dolphins leap in tight, corkscrew spins that can launch them high above the waves. They can spin up to 7 times in the air.

thresher-shark.description: A thresher shark is a sleek, fast-swimming ocean predator famous for its extraordinarily long, whip-like tail that it uses to stun prey.

goblin-shark.description: The goblin shark is a rare, deep-sea species recognized by its long snout and slingshot-like jaws that extend to capture prey

gulper-eel.description: The gulper eel's enormous mouth and expandable throat can engulf prey. A tiny light-producing organ sits at the tip of its long, whip-like tail.
gulper-eel.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

deep-sea-skate.description: Found in extreme depths of up to 3km, these resilient marine creatures gracefully glide over the ocean floor to hunt for bottom dwellers.

chimera.description: The rabbitfish is a chimaera with a cartilage skeleton, a long tapering tail, and permanent tooth plates for crushing shellfish.
chimera.measurementNote: Reference maximum size for the rabbitfish, a species of chimaera.

frilled-shark.description: Six pairs of frilly gill slits give this deep-water shark its name. Its eel-like body and rows of three-pointed teeth help it capture prey.
frilled-shark.measurementNote: Upper length and weight from a study of female sharks; the two values were not measured on the same individual.

cookie-cutter-shark.description: Cookiecutter sharks use thick lips to grip larger animals and sharp lower teeth to cut round plugs of flesh. Their undersides glow with bioluminescence.

silky-shark.description: A swift, pelagic shark that gets its name from its exceptionally smooth, soft skin, which is covered in densely packed overlapping scales.

oceanic-whitetip-shark.description: Long, rounded pectoral fins and white-tipped fins distinguish this open-ocean shark. It searches warm seas for fish, squid, and other food.

blue-shark-oceanic.description: Blue sharks make long migrations through temperate and tropical seas. Their slender bodies and long pectoral fins suit life in the open ocean.

galapagos-shark.description: Galapagos sharks favor clear, warm water around oceanic islands. These large requiem sharks patrol reef edges and feed mainly on fish.

yellowfin-tuna.description: They utilize a biological hydraulic system that pumps fluid into their fins, instantly stiffening them to execute razor-sharp, high-speed turns.

sailfish.description: Sailfish use their long bills to slash or tap schooling prey. They raise their large dorsal fins while hunting and fold them down when swimming quickly.

wahoo.description: Wahoo are streamlined predators with sharp teeth and blue bars along their sides. They hunt fish and squid in warm ocean waters.

loggerhead-sea-turtle.description: Loggerheads use large heads and powerful jaws to crush crabs, whelks, and other hard-shelled prey. Adults travel widely between feeding and nesting areas.

nurse-shark.description: Nurse sharks can rest completely still on the ocean floor and pump water directly over their gills to breathe, unlike many other shark species.

yellow-lipped-sea-krait.description: Yellow-lipped sea kraits hunt eels underwater with potent venom. Unlike fully aquatic sea snakes, they come ashore to rest, digest meals, and lay eggs.

emerald-crab.description: Emerald crabs prowl at night, picking algae and leftovers with spoon-tipped claws. Their leafy green shell hides them among corals.

sea-urchin.description: Long-spined sea urchins graze on algae and help keep reef surfaces clear. Their slender spines defend them while tube feet grip and move over rocks.
sea-urchin.measurementNote: Test means the hard body, excluding spines. Weight is a rounded study mean for adults with 2.4–3.1 in tests.

anemone.description: The magnificent anemone anchors to reef rock with a sticky foot. Its stinging tentacles catch prey and shelter several species of anemonefish.
anemone.measurementNote: A typical disc width and the weight of a published 357 g specimen; these are separate reference measurements.

blue-crab.description: Blue crabs swim with paddle-shaped rear legs. They shed their shells to grow, leaving them briefly soft until the new shell hardens.

arrow-crab.description: Arrow crabs tiptoe on stilt-like legs, their long “arrow” snout probing crevices. At night they scavenge around for leftovers.
arrow-crab.measurementNote: Weight is the approximate mean of 247 crabs in a survey. The larger leg-span reference is not paired with that weight.

mantis-shrimp.description: Peacock mantis shrimp smash hard-shelled prey with club-like limbs. Their rapid strikes create cavitation bubbles that collapse in a second impact.
mantis-shrimp.measurementNote: Upper reference length and weight for the peacock mantis shrimp.

leather-starfish.description: Leather stars have smooth, rubbery skin and a garlic-like odor. Tube feet carry them over rocky Pacific shores as they feed on anemones and other prey.
leather-starfish.measurementNote: Weight is a published population estimate; the span is an upper size reference, not a paired measurement.

cleaner-shrimp.description: Scarlet cleaner shrimp wave long white antennae at cleaning stations. Fish visit to have parasites and dead tissue removed from their skin and mouths.
cleaner-shrimp.measurementNote: Rounded mean length and whole weight of 336 shrimp in a study.

crown-of-thorns.description: Crown-of-thorns sea stars spread their stomachs over corals to digest living tissue outside their bodies. Venomous spines help deter predators.

nudibranch.description: The magnificent chromodoris is a brightly patterned, sponge-eating sea slug. Chemicals obtained from its food help defend it against predators.
nudibranch.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

giant-triton.description: Giant tritons are large predatory sea snails that hunt crown-of-thorns starfish, subduing them with a paralyzing bite.
giant-triton.measurementNote: Measurements printed on the approved Giant Triton card, updated November 8, 2026.

octopus.description: Day octopuses hunt on reefs in daylight, changing color and skin texture to blend into their surroundings.
octopus.measurementNote: Rounded upper reference length (about 80 cm, including arms) and weight (4.5 kg); separate aquarium references, not a matched individual.

oysters.description: Eastern oysters filter plankton from coastal water. Their rough shells grow together into reefs that shelter fish, crabs, and other small animals.
oysters.measurementNote: Rounded mean shell length and whole weight of 3,653 eastern oysters; includes the shell.

giant-clam.description: Giant clams are the largest living bivalves. Living in warm, shallow coral reefs, they anchor themselves and rely on symbiotic algae for much of their energy.

deep-cucumber.description: The swimming sea cucumber feeds on seafloor sediment, then swims with a webbed veil. Its transparent body reveals the coiled gut inside.
deep-cucumber.measurementNote: Rounded mean length and wet body weight of 58 swimming sea cucumbers.

brittlestar.description: Common brittle stars raise their spiny arms to catch food particles from passing water. A lost arm can regrow after a narrow escape.
brittlestar.measurementNote: Disc width excludes the arms. Weight is a rounded estimate from a published wet-weight graph.

vampire-squid.description: When threatened, it doesn't ink; instead, it cloaks itself by pulling its webbed arms over its head and releases glowing, bioluminescent clouds.
vampire-squid.measurementNote: A published estimate for experimental specimens; not a maximum weight.

giant-isopod.description: Giant isopods are deep-sea relatives of woodlice. Their armored bodies protect them as they scavenge, and a slow metabolism helps them endure long fasts.
giant-isopod.measurementNote: Rounded upper length and weight from an Exuma Sound sample.

giant-tube-worm.description: Giant tube worms live at hydrothermal vents. Without a mouth or gut, adults rely on internal bacteria that use chemicals from vent fluids to make food.
giant-tube-worm.measurementNote: Length describes the tube; weight describes the living worm without its tube.

peacock-squid.description: Boreal glass squid have transparent bodies and large eyes. Light organs beneath the eyes help conceal their silhouettes in the dim ocean.
peacock-squid.measurementNote: Rounded mean mantle length and whole weight of two boreal glass squid. Mantle length excludes arms and tentacles.

deep-sea-jelly.description: Atolla jellyfish can flash rings of blue bioluminescence when disturbed. This burglar-alarm display may draw larger predators toward an attacker.
deep-sea-jelly.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

dumbo-octopus.description: To hunt they hover right above the seafloor and "hoover" up worms, snails, and crustaceans, swallowing their prey whole.
dumbo-octopus.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

giant-red-shrimp.description: Famous for its vivid, deep red coloration, extremely long antennae, and a prominent crest.

man-o-war.description: A Portuguese man o' war is a colony of specialized zooids. Its gas-filled float rides at the surface while long, stinging tentacles capture prey below.
man-o-war.measurementNote: Weight is a study mean for small colonies. The long tentacle reference describes larger colonies and is not paired with this weight.

blue-sea-dragon.description: Blue sea dragons float upside down at the surface. They eat animals such as the Portuguese man o' war and store stolen stinging cells for defense.
blue-sea-dragon.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

market-squid.description: Market squid live only about six to nine months. They gather to mate and lay egg capsules on the seafloor, then die after spawning.
market-squid.measurementNote: Length includes arms; weight is a published maximum.

box-jellyfish.description: The Australian box jellyfish has a cube-shaped bell and clusters of eyes. Its long tentacles carry powerful venom for catching fish and shrimp.
box-jellyfish.measurementNote: Length describes bell width; weight is a published maximum.

lionfish.description: Lionfish spread their broad fins to corner small fish before striking. Their defensive spines are venomous; introduced populations threaten Atlantic reefs.

winter-flounder.description: Flounders lie flat and camouflaged, burying in sand with both eyes on one side. They ambush prey with a sudden snap.

cleaner-wrasse.description: Cleaner wrasses run reef “stations” where big fish queue for a cleanup. They pick off parasites and dead skin—earning a safe meal and trust.

fairy-parrotfish.description: Singapore parrotfish graze reef surfaces with fused, beak-like teeth. Terminal-phase fish have a distinctive green throat and brightly edged scales.
fairy-parrotfish.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

bluestriped-grunt.description: Bluestriped grunts gather over reefs by day and feed over sand and seagrass at night. They make grunting sounds by rubbing their throat teeth.

clownfish.description: Bearing bright orange and white markings, they are renowned for their unique ability to safely live inside venomous sea anemones without getting stung.

spanish-hogfish.description: Young Spanish hogfish clean parasites from other fish. Adults feed on bottom-dwelling invertebrates, and some females later change into males.

picasso-triggerfish.description: Known for its striking colors and pugnacious attitude, this triggerfish can lock its dorsal spine into coral crevices for protection.

porcupine-fish.description: Porcupinefish puff into a spiky ball to scare off predators. Their beak crushes shells, and some species carry a powerful toxin.

french-angelfish.description: French angelfish cruise reefs in bonded pairs, flashing yellow-edged scales and a dark mask.

sargeant-major.description: Sergeant major damselfish wear bold black-and-white bars with a splash of yellow on top. Males fiercely guard egg patches.

longhorn-cowfish.description: Protected by a rigid, box-like body, longhorn cowfish graze on small bottom-dwelling prey. When severely stressed, they can release toxic mucus.
longhorn-cowfish.measurementNote: Fork length ends at the fork in the tail. Weight is estimated from a published length–weight relationship.

spotfin-butterflyfish.description: A black spot near the rear of the dorsal fin gives the spotfin butterflyfish its name. A dark stripe crosses its eye as it forages around reefs.

queen-angelfish.description: The Queen Angelfish is a brilliantly colored reef fish that glides through warm, clear Caribbean shallows, recognizable by its vivid colors.

blue-tang.description: An active herbivore that shifts between territorial, wandering, and schooling social phases. It grazes continuously on algae.

frogfish.description: Giant frogfish blend into sponges and reef growth, then lure prey with a modified fin spine. An expanding mouth pulls the victim in with a sudden gulp.
frogfish.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

spectacled-parrotfish.description: Known for its distinctive “spectacle-like” markings around the eyes and beak, it contributes to sand production through its feeding.

bristlemouth.description: Bristlemouths are tiny deep-sea fish considered the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, with populations in the quadrillions.

owlfish.description: These stealthy predators drift through pitch-black environments using their massive eyes to spot the faintest glimmers of bioluminescent prey.

pacific-grenadier.description: Often called a "rattail" because of its slender, whip-like tail, this deep-sea fish can live for over 70 years in extreme pressures.
pacific-grenadier.measurementNote: Rounded published maximum length and weight.

viperfish.description: Long, needle-like teeth help viperfish hold slippery prey. Light-producing organs on their bodies and dorsal-fin lure shine in the deep sea.

humpback-anglerfish.description: Female humpback anglerfish carry a lure lit by symbiotic bacteria. It dangles above the mouth, drawing prey close in the darkness of the deep sea.
humpback-anglerfish.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

barrel-eye-fish.description: A transparent dome protects the barreleye's tubular green eyes. The eyes can rotate from looking upward to facing forward as the fish feeds.
barrel-eye-fish.measurementNote: A reliable whole-body weight was not located in the reviewed species references. The length remains a separate, sourced measurement.

fangtooth-fish.description: Fangtooth fish have enormous teeth for their small bodies. Special sockets in the roof of the mouth make room for the long lower fangs.
fangtooth-fish.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

black-swallower.description: The black swallower has an elastic stomach that can hold prey larger than itself. This adaptation helps it take advantage of scarce deep-sea meals.
black-swallower.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

tripod-fish.description: Tripod fish stand above the seabed on three elongated fin rays. Facing into the current, they spread their pectoral fins to help detect drifting prey.
tripod-fish.measurementNote: Weight is an estimate from a published length–weight model at the listed length.

coelacanth.description: West Indian Ocean coelacanths have fleshy, lobed fins and a distinctive three-part tail. These deep-water fish belong to an ancient lineage.

flying-fish.description: It escapes underwater predators by rocketing to the surface and using its rigid, wing-like fins to glide gracefully through the air for hundreds of feet.

barracuda-oceanic.description: Barracudas wait near prey before lunging with bursts of speed. Their streamlined bodies and sharp teeth help them catch other fish.

mahi-mahi.description: Mahi-mahi grow rapidly in warm ocean waters. They hunt fish and squid, often gathering near floating seaweed, logs, and other objects.

king-mackerel.description: A highly sought-after, migratory coastal pelagic fish that is renowned for "skyrocketing" clear out of the water when aggressively attacking prey.

tripletail.description: The tripletail is a master of surface deception. It drifts sideways to mimic floating dead leaves and fool its prey.

halfbeak.description: Ballyhoo halfbeaks swim near the surface with a long lower jaw and a short upper jaw. They feed on drifting plants and small animals.
halfbeak.measurementNote: Rounded mean length and whole weight of 432 ballyhoo halfbeaks in a study.

needlefish.description: Hound needlefish hunt near the surface with long jaws lined with sharp teeth. They chase small fish and may leap clear of the water.
needlefish.measurementNote: Rounded published maximum length and weight for the hound needlefish.

bluefin-tuna-juvenile.description: Young Atlantic bluefin tuna grow quickly and gather in schools. They eat small fish, squid, and crustaceans as they develop into powerful ocean hunters.

remora.description: A modified dorsal fin forms the remora's suction disc. It attaches to larger marine animals for transport and feeds on scraps or parasites.

bluefish.description: Bluefish are the only living species in the family Pomatomidae. Schools of these sharp-toothed predators pursue smaller fish in coastal waters.

bonito-tuna.description: Bonitos are streamlined relatives of tunas and mackerels. They hunt small schooling fish, squid, and crustaceans in open coastal waters.

crevalle-jack.description: Crevalle jacks are powerful coastal predators that often hunt in schools. They can make grunting sounds using their teeth and swim bladder.

yellowtail-amberjack.description: Yellowtail amberjacks are strong-swimming predators with a yellow tail and side stripe. They school around rocky reefs and hunt fish and squid.

frigate-tuna.description: Frigate tuna form large schools in warm seas. They pursue small fish, squid, and crustaceans and may also feed on members of their own species.

lookdown.description: The lookdown gets its name from its steep forehead and high-set eyes. Its thin, silvery body reflects light as it swims in coastal schools.

pompano.description: Florida pompano forage over sandy bottoms for small crustaceans and mollusks. These silvery fish often travel in schools along the surf zone.

ocean-triggerfish.description: Ocean triggerfish swim above reefs and drop-offs, feeding on plankton and small animals. They can lock their first dorsal spine upright for defense.

african-pompano.description: Young African pompano trail long, thread-like fin rays that resemble jellyfish tentacles. These streamers shorten as the fish grow into silvery adults.

krill-bloom-base.description: Antarctic krill gather in dense swarms that feed whales, seals, and penguins. Length and weight describe one krill.
krill-bloom-base.measurementNote: Length and weight describe one Antarctic krill, rounded from published average ranges.

krill-bloom-stage1.description: Antarctic krill gather in dense swarms that feed whales, seals, and penguins. Length and weight describe one krill.
krill-bloom-stage1.measurementNote: Length and weight describe one Antarctic krill, rounded from published average ranges.

krill-bloom-stage2.description: Antarctic krill gather in dense swarms that feed whales, seals, and penguins. Length and weight describe one krill.
krill-bloom-stage2.measurementNote: Length and weight describe one Antarctic krill, rounded from published average ranges.

sardine-ball-base.description: Pacific sardines form dense schools and feed on plankton. Length and weight describe one fish, not the entire school.
sardine-ball-base.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

anchovy-ball-base.description: Northern anchovies feed on plankton and school together near the coast. Length and weight describe one fish.
anchovy-ball-base.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

silverside-ball-base.description: Atlantic silversides form shimmering schools in shallow coastal water. Length and weight describe one fish.
silverside-ball-base.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

sardine-ball-stage1.description: Pacific sardines form dense schools and feed on plankton. Length and weight describe one fish, not the entire school.
sardine-ball-stage1.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

anchovy-ball-stage1.description: Northern anchovies feed on plankton and school together near the coast. Length and weight describe one fish.
anchovy-ball-stage1.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

silverside-ball-stage1.description: Atlantic silversides form shimmering schools in shallow coastal water. Length and weight describe one fish.
silverside-ball-stage1.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

sardine-ball-stage2.description: Pacific sardines form dense schools and feed on plankton. Length and weight describe one fish, not the entire school.
sardine-ball-stage2.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

anchovy-ball-stage2.description: Northern anchovies feed on plankton and school together near the coast. Length and weight describe one fish.
anchovy-ball-stage2.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

silverside-ball-stage2.description: Atlantic silversides form shimmering schools in shallow coastal water. Length and weight describe one fish.
silverside-ball-stage2.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

herring-ball-base.description: Atlantic herring travel in schools between feeding and spawning grounds. Length and weight describe one fish.
herring-ball-base.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

herring-ball-stage1.description: Atlantic herring travel in schools between feeding and spawning grounds. Length and weight describe one fish.
herring-ball-stage1.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

herring-ball-stage2.description: Atlantic herring travel in schools between feeding and spawning grounds. Length and weight describe one fish.
herring-ball-stage2.measurementNote: Length and estimated weight describe one fish. Weight is calculated from a published length–weight model.

white-grunt.description: White grunts school around reefs by day and forage at night. They make low grunting sounds by rubbing teeth in their throats.

emperor-angelfish.description: When startled, adult emperor angelfishes can produce a loud, audible thumping or knocking sound that resembles a drum roll.

flounder.description: Flounders lie flat and camouflaged, burying in sand with both eyes on one side. They ambush prey with a sudden snap.
